title: Tres Leches Cake
subtitle: light sponge soaked in three milks, topped with whipped cream
excerpt: Tres leches cake is a light vanilla sponge that is baked, pierced all over and soaked in a mixture of whole milk, evaporated milk and condensed milk until saturated and deeply moist. It is finished with whipped cream and needs at least 4 hours in the fridge to set. This is a make-ahead dessert that improves overnight.
sourceNotes: Tres leches cake is popular across Latin America and is particularly associated with Mexico and Nicaragua. The recipe became widespread after sweetened condensed milk producers printed it on tins in the mid-twentieth century.

glossaryTerms.definition: Spanish for three milks. In this cake the baked sponge is soaked in a mixture of whole milk, evaporated milk and condensed milk, making it intensely moist.

content.text: This recipe serves 12 and requires 30 minutes of baking plus at least 4 hours of chilling before serving. The sponge is intentionally light so it absorbs the milk mixture without becoming heavy. Do not skip the chilling time.

soaking mixture is made with 240 ml whole milk, 240 ml evaporated milk and the full tin of condensed milk. Mix them together before the cake comes out of the oven so you are ready to pour it on while the sponge is still warm. A warm sponge absorbs liquid far more readily than a cold one.
Heat the oven to 180°C. Grease a 23 cm x 33 cm baking tin thoroughly with butter and line the base with baking paper.

Whip the egg whites in a large clean bowl with a hand mixer until they hold stiff peaks. In a separate large bowl, beat the egg yolks with the caster sugar until the mixture is pale, thick and has roughly doubled in volume, about 3 to 4 minutes. Add 1 teaspoon of vanilla extract to the yolks and mix briefly.

Sift the flour over the yolk mixture and fold gently with a large spatula until just combined. Add the melted butter and fold again. Now fold in the whipped egg whites in three additions, working gently to keep the batter airy. Stop folding when no white streaks remain.
Pour the batter into the prepared tin. Smooth the top. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the sponge is golden, springs back when pressed lightly and a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean.
While the cake bakes, mix the three milks together in a jug: the condensed milk, 240 ml of evaporated milk and 240 ml of whole milk. Stir well.

As soon as the sponge comes out of the oven, use a skewer to poke holes all over the surface, spacing them about 2 cm apart. Pour the milk mixture slowly and evenly over the hot sponge, letting it absorb before pouring more. Use all of it. The sponge will look very wet. This is correct.
Leave the cake to cool to room temperature in its tin, then cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or overnight.

Before serving, whip 300 ml of double cream with 1 tablespoon of caster sugar and a few drops of vanilla extract until it holds soft peaks. Spread over the top of the chilled cake. Cut into squares and serve directly from the tin.

attrs.symptom: The sponge did not absorb the milk mixture and it has pooled at the bottom of the tin.
attrs.cause: The cake was too cold when the milk was poured, or not enough holes were made.
attrs.fix: Pour the milk mixture as soon as the cake comes out of the oven while it is still hot. Poke plenty of deep holes close together.

attrs.symptom: The sponge is dense rather than light.
attrs.cause: The egg whites were under-whipped or deflated by over-folding.
attrs.fix: Whip the whites to proper stiff peaks and fold with a light hand. Stop folding the moment the whites are incorporated.

attrs.symptom: The whipped cream topping has gone watery before serving.
attrs.cause: The cream was not whipped firmly enough, or the cake was at room temperature when the cream was added.
attrs.fix: Make sure the cake is fully chilled before adding the cream. Whip to soft peaks that hold their shape before spreading.

content.text: Tres leches cake is made across Mexico, Nicaragua and much of Latin America. It is a celebration cake, served at birthdays and family gatherings. The recipe became popular when it appeared on tins of condensed milk. It is a good make-ahead dessert because it must be chilled and it keeps well in the fridge for two days.
